notes: The house art style (docs/15_vehicle_preparation_pipeline.md#D15-S9).
Every vehicle in this game is downloaded art by a different artist with a different idea of
what a car looks like. One is a photoscanned supercar, the next a flat-shaded cartoon with
primary-colour paint and no textures at all. Dropped in side by side they read as two games.
This table is what makes them read as one. It is applied per MATERIAL, in Blender, before any
geometry is touched, and it does exactly one thing: it moves every surface's colour and its
reflectance into a band the whole roster shares. Grimy, desaturated, weathered metal under a
sodium-lit sky; paint that has been outdoors for a decade; chrome that has gone dull; glass
that is dirty. Realistic rather than stylised, dark rather than bright, worn rather than new.
It does NOT touch the properties the labelling ensemble reads as evidence (D15-S4.2 C2): a
material's alpha mode, its transmission, its backface culling and its NAME survive the pass
untouched. Normalising those would make every windscreen opaque and every glass cue useless,
which is the one way this pass could break the pipeline that runs after it.
Colour bands are HSV. saturationMax and value[Min,Max] are clamps, not assignments: a red car
stays a red car, it just stops being a TOY red car. hueShiftDeg is applied first and exists so
a surface whose real-world hue is not a free choice -- rust, sodium light -- can be pinned.
grime is how far the clamped colour is then dragged toward grimeColour. It is the difference
between a clean render and something that has been driven through a scrapyard.

surfaces.notes: Hue is preserved -- a faction colour is gameplay. Saturation and value are not: a 1.0/1.0 cartoon red becomes an oxidised 0.45/0.42 one.

surfaces.displayName: Everything the pass could not identify
surfaces.notes: The fallback, and the most important row in the table. On a real car most materials are body-coloured panels and details that no cue names, and forcing them into the trim band -- near-black, non-metallic, rough -- turns the whole vehicle into grey mush and erases an alloy wheel's spokes outright. So this row barely moves anything: it clamps a cartoon's saturation, adds a little dirt, and leaves metallic and roughness exactly as the artist set them. A null means preserve.

Almost achromatic. Unpainted plastic on a real vehicle is grey-black and goes chalky, and it is the surface that most gives a cartoon model away. Only a material a cue actually IDENTIFIED as trim lands here -- anything unrecognised takes the neutral row above, which is a different and much gentler thing.
Roughness well above a showroom 0.05: dull, pitted, slightly warm. Mirror chrome is the single strongest 'this is a render' signal there is.
Transmission and alpha are NOT written here -- they are labelling evidence (D15-R6). Only the tint and the surface roughness are.
Near black, entirely rough, heavily dusted. A tyre rendered as dark grey plastic is the second strongest render signal.
The one surface allowed to stay bright, because a lamp that is not brighter than the car around it does not read as a lamp. Emission strength is preserved rather than rewritten.
Dark, half metallic and filthy. A grille collects everything the road throws at it.
Barely visible through glazing in play, and dark enough that it never draws the eye away from the exterior.
The hue shift is deliberate and is toward rust. Nothing under a vehicle in this game has ever been washed.

notes: How the pass decides whether it is looking at a cartoon or at a photoscan, and therefore
how hard to push. Both numbers are measured over the scene's materials, weighted by the
triangles each one covers, so one stray bright badge cannot make a realistic car cartoon.
A stylised source is REPLACED: its base-colour textures are disconnected and the flat house
colour takes over, which is what 'reskinned into my style' means for a model whose textures
are flat colour anyway. A realistic source is only PULLED toward the palette by
realisticStrength, because its textures carry detail worth keeping.
